# Language: Georgian (ka)

---

**Transliteration standard:** National System of Georgia (2002), as used in Georgian passports and official romanization, supplemented by standard academic convention for Georgian studies. Applied consistently throughout.

---

**1.**
**Form:** ჭეშმარიტი
**Transliteration:** č̣ešmariti
**Literal meaning:** root č̣ešmar- (truth, genuine quality) + adjectival suffix -i
**Typical English translations:** true, truthful, genuine, real
**Usage:** Used to predicate truth of statements and propositions, as well as genuineness of persons or things. Appears in philosophical, theological, and everyday contexts. Participates in derivation: č̣ešmariteba (truth, as abstract noun).
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**2.**
**Form:** ჭეშმარიტება
**Transliteration:** č̣ešmariteba
**Literal meaning:** č̣ešmariti + nominalizing suffix -eba
**Typical English translations:** truth, truthfulness, veracity
**Usage:** The standard abstract noun for truth in Georgian, used across philosophical, religious, legal, and everyday registers. Commonly appears as the subject or object of predications about what is the case. Central to Georgian theological and philosophical writing.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**3.**
**Form:** სიმართლე
**Transliteration:** simartle
**Literal meaning:** si- (nominal prefix) + martal- (right, correct, just) + -e (nominal suffix)
**Typical English translations:** truth, correctness, rightness, justice
**Usage:** Overlaps with č̣ešmariteba but is more commonly used in everyday speech for factual truth and in legal or moral contexts for rightness and justice. The phrase simartle tkva ("told the truth") is highly frequent. Also used in the sense of what is factually accurate in a dispute.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**4.**
**Form:** მართალი
**Transliteration:** martali
**Literal meaning:** martal- (right, correct) + adjectival suffix -i
**Typical English translations:** right, correct, truthful, just, innocent
**Usage:** Applied to persons (a truthful or just person), statements (a correct claim), and verdicts (a just outcome). In legal contexts can carry the sense of innocent or vindicated. Closely related to simartle through shared root.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**5.**
**Form:** სიყალბე
**Transliteration:** siq̇albe
**Literal meaning:** si- + q̇alb- (false, counterfeit) + -e
**Typical English translations:** falseness, falsehood, forgery, inauthenticity
**Usage:** Used for the abstract quality of being false or counterfeit, applicable to documents, currency, statements, and persons. Frequently appears in legal contexts involving forgery or fraud. Antonym of simartle and č̣ešmariteba.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**6.**
**Form:** ყალბი
**Transliteration:** q̇albi
**Literal meaning:** q̇alb- (false, counterfeit) + adjectival suffix -i; borrowed from Persian/Arabic via Turkish
**Typical English translations:** false, fake, counterfeit, forged
**Usage:** The standard adjective for counterfeit or forged items (q̇albi dokumenti, "forged document") and false statements. Also used colloquially for inauthentic behavior or persons. Productive in derivation: siq̇albe, q̇alboba.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**7.**
**Form:** ნამდვილი
**Transliteration:** namdvili
**Literal meaning:** nam- (perfective preverb functioning as intensifier in this lexicalized form) + dvil- (root related to being, existence) + -i
**Typical English translations:** real, genuine, authentic, actual, true
**Usage:** The primary adjective for authenticity and genuineness of objects, persons, and states of affairs. Namdvili oqro ("real gold"), namdvili megobari ("true friend"). Widely used across registers and participates in productive derivation (namdviloba, "genuineness, authenticity").
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**8.**
**Form:** ნამდვილობა
**Transliteration:** namdviloba
**Literal meaning:** namdvili + nominalizing suffix -oba
**Typical English translations:** authenticity, genuineness, realness
**Usage:** Abstract noun derived from namdvili, used in legal, administrative, and philosophical contexts to refer to the property of being genuine or authentic. Appears in discussions of document verification and identity.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**9.**
**Form:** სიცრუე
**Transliteration:** sicrue
**Literal meaning:** si- + cru- (lie, false) + -e
**Typical English translations:** lie, falsehood, untruth
**Usage:** The standard noun for a lie or falsehood in everyday and moral discourse. Contrasts with simartle. Used in moral evaluation of persons and statements. The verb tkuili tkva ("told a lie") is a near-synonym construction; sicrue is the more abstract nominal form.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**10.**
**Form:** ტყუილი
**Transliteration:** ẗq̇uili
**Literal meaning:** ẗq̇uil- (lie, falsehood) + nominal suffix -i
**Typical English translations:** lie, falsehood, untruth
**Usage:** The most common everyday word for a lie, used in direct moral evaluation of statements and persons. Slightly more colloquial than sicrue. The verb ẗq̇uili tkva is a standard fixed expression meaning "told a lie." Also used adverbially in the sense of "in vain, for nothing."
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**11.**
**Form:** სარწმუნო
**Transliteration:** sarwmuno
**Literal meaning:** sa- (circumfix, "worthy of") + rwmun- (belief, trust, faith) + -o
**Typical English translations:** credible, reliable, trustworthy, believable
**Usage:** Applied to persons, sources, testimony, and evidence to indicate that they merit belief or trust. Frequently used in legal and journalistic contexts. Participates in derivation: sarwmunoba ("credibility, reliability").
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**12.**
**Form:** სარწმუნოება
**Transliteration:** sarwmunoeba
**Literal meaning:** sarwmuno + nominalizing suffix -eba
**Typical English translations:** credibility, reliability, trustworthiness; also faith, religion (in theological register)
**Usage:** In secular contexts, denotes the property of being credible or trustworthy. In theological and ecclesiastical contexts, the dominant meaning shifts to faith or religion. The semantic range is broad and context-dependent.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**13.**
**Form:** დამაჯერებელი
**Transliteration:** damajerebeliˈ
**Literal meaning:** da- (preverb) + majer- (causative of "believe") + -ebeli (agentive/adjectival suffix, "capable of causing")
**Typical English translations:** convincing, persuasive, credible, plausible
**Usage:** Applied to arguments, evidence, persons, and performances to indicate that they are capable of producing belief or conviction. Commonly used in legal, rhetorical, and critical contexts. Distinct from sarwmuno in emphasizing the effect on a hearer rather than an intrinsic property.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**14.**
**Form:** სანდო
**Transliteration:** sando
**Literal meaning:** sa- + nd- (root of trust, confidence) + -o
**Typical English translations:** trustworthy, reliable, dependable
**Usage:** Applied primarily to persons and sources to indicate reliability and trustworthiness. Frequently used in contexts of evaluating witnesses, informants, and institutions. Closely synonymous with sarwmuno but may carry a slightly stronger interpersonal connotation of personal trust.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**15.**
**Form:** უტყუარი
**Transliteration:** uẗq̇uari
**Literal meaning:** u- (privative prefix, "without") + ẗq̇uar- (lie, falsehood) + -i
**Typical English translations:** infallible, indubitable, certain, irrefutable
**Usage:** Used to describe evidence, proofs, or facts that are beyond doubt or cannot be falsified. Appears in legal and philosophical contexts. The privative formation explicitly marks the absence of falsehood or error.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**16.**
**Form:** ავთენტური
**Transliteration:** avt̕ent̕uri
**Literal meaning:** borrowed from Greek/Latin authenticus via European languages + adjectival suffix -uri
**Typical English translations:** authentic
**Usage:** A loanword used primarily in formal, legal, archival, and academic contexts to describe documents, texts, or objects whose origin and integrity are verified. Less common in everyday speech than namdvili, which covers similar ground in informal registers.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**17.**
**Form:** ლეგიტიმური
**Transliteration:** legitimuri
**Literal meaning:** borrowed from Latin/European legitimus + adjectival suffix -uri
**Typical English translations:** legitimate, lawful, valid
**Usage:** Used in legal, political, and institutional contexts to evaluate whether authority, claims, or actions conform to recognized rules or norms. Distinct from mere legality in sometimes carrying a normative or moral dimension.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**18.**
**Form:** კანონიერი
**Transliteration:** kanonieri
**Literal meaning:** kanon- (law, rule; from Greek kanon) + -ieri (adjectival suffix, "having the quality of")
**Typical English translations:** lawful, legal, legitimate, rightful
**Usage:** The standard adjective for legality and lawfulness in Georgian legal discourse. Applied to actions, claims, ownership, and authority. Overlaps with legitimuri but is more specifically tied to positive law rather than broader normative legitimacy.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**19.**
**Form:** სამართლიანი
**Transliteration:** samart̕liani
**Literal meaning:** samart̕al- (law, justice, right) + -iani (adjectival suffix, "characterized by")
**Typical English translations:** just, fair, righteous, equitable
**Usage:** Applied to persons, decisions, distributions, and systems to evaluate them as conforming to standards of justice or fairness. Central to moral and legal evaluation in Georgian. Participates in productive derivation: samart̕lianoba ("justice, fairness").
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**20.**
**Form:** სამართლიანობა
**Transliteration:** samart̕lianoba
**Literal meaning:** samart̕liani + nominalizing suffix -oba
**Typical English translations:** justice, fairness, righteousness, equity
**Usage:** The abstract noun for justice and fairness, used in philosophical, legal, and political discourse. A central term in Georgian ethical and legal vocabulary.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**21.**
**Form:** მიმსგავსება
**Transliteration:** mimsgavseba
**Literal meaning:** mi- (preverb) + msgavs- (similar, resembling) + -eba (verbal/nominal suffix)
**Typical English translations:** resemblance, likening, assimilation (to a model)
**Usage:** Refers to the process or result of making something resemble something else, or the state of resemblance. Used in aesthetic and theological contexts (e.g., resemblance to a divine model). Less common in everyday speech.
**Epistemic status:** [MARGINAL]

---

**22.**
**Form:** მსგავსი
**Transliteration:** msgavsi
**Literal meaning:** msgavs- (similar, like) + adjectival suffix -i
**Typical English translations:** similar, like, resembling
**Usage:** The standard adjective for similarity and resemblance, used across registers. Applied to persons, objects, and situations. Participates in derivation: msgavseba ("similarity, resemblance, likeness").
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**23.**
**Form:** გულწრფელი
**Transliteration:** gulwrp̕eli
**Literal meaning:** gul- (heart) + wrp̕el- (straight, sincere) + -i; literally "straight-hearted"
**Typical English translations:** sincere, genuine, frank, candid
**Usage:** Applied to persons and expressions to indicate sincerity and absence of deception. Used in moral evaluation of character and in assessing the authenticity of emotional or verbal expression. Contrasts with terms implying hypocrisy or pretense.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**24.**
**Form:** თვალთმაქცობა
**Transliteration:** t̕valt̕maq̇c̕oba
**Literal meaning:** t̕val- (eye) + t̕maq̇c̕- (deceiver, juggler) + -oba (nominalizing suffix); literally "eye-deceiving"
**Typical English translations:** deception, hypocrisy, pretense, charlatanism
**Usage:** Refers to deliberate deception through appearance or performance, including hypocrisy and charlatanism. Used in moral condemnation of persons who present a false appearance. The morphological structure explicitly encodes visual deception.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**25.**
**Form:** შესაბამისი
**Transliteration:** šesabamisi
**Literal meaning:** še- (preverb) + sabam- (correspondence, conformity) + -isi (adjectival suffix)
**Typical English translations:** corresponding, conforming, appropriate, consistent with
**Usage:** Used to evaluate whether something conforms to or corresponds with a standard, rule, or expectation. Appears in legal, administrative, and evaluative contexts. Relevant to assessments of whether conduct or representations match what is required or claimed.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**26.**
**Form:** ზუსტი
**Transliteration:** zusti
**Literal meaning:** zust- (exact, precise; loanword from Persian/Turkish) + adjectival suffix -i
**Typical English translations:** exact, precise, accurate
**Usage:** Applied to measurements, translations, statements, and reproductions to indicate precision and accuracy. Widely used across technical, scientific, and everyday registers. Participates in derivation: zustoba, zustad ("precisely, exactly" as adverb).
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**27.**
**Form:** სიზუსტე
**Transliteration:** sizuste
**Literal meaning:** si- + zust- + -e
**Typical English translations:** exactness, precision, accuracy
**Usage:** Abstract noun for the property of being exact or accurate. Used in technical, scientific, and evaluative contexts. Closely related to zusti through shared root.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**28.**
**Form:** გარეგნული
**Transliteration:** garegnuli
**Literal meaning:** gareg- (outer, external) + -nuli (adjectival suffix)
**Typical English translations:** external, outward, superficial, apparent
**Usage:** Used to mark a contrast between outward appearance and inner reality or essence. Relevant in contexts where the reliability of surface appearances is evaluated. Often implicitly contrasted with šinagani ("internal, inner").
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**29.**
**Form:** არსებითი
**Transliteration:** arsebiti
**Literal meaning:** arseb- (being, existence, essence; from arsi, "essence") + -iti (adjectival suffix)
**Typical English translations:** essential, substantial, fundamental, material
**Usage:** Applied to qualities, differences, and facts to indicate that they pertain to the fundamental nature or essence of something. Used in philosophical, legal, and evaluative contexts. In legal usage, arsebiti gansxvaveba ("material difference") is a recognized expression.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

---

**30.**
**Form:** ფსევდო-
**Transliteration:** psevdo-
**Literal meaning:** borrowed from Greek pseudos (false) + productive prefix in Georgian
**Typical English translations:** pseudo-, false, spurious (as prefix)
**Usage:** A productive borrowed prefix attached to nouns to indicate that something falsely presents itself as belonging to a category. Used in academic, journalistic, and critical registers (e.g., psevdomecnieri, "pseudo-scientist"). Marks inauthenticity of classification or identity.
**Epistemic status:** [CORE]

# Language: Georgian (ka)

---

## Step 1 — Identify Central Roots

---

**Root 1**

**Form:** მართ- / marṭ-
**Transliteration:** mart-
**P1 participation:** 4 items — martali (#4), simartle (#3), samart̕liani (#19), samart̕lianoba (#20)
**Core meaning contribution:** Rightness, correctness, and justice as aligned with a standard — covering factual accuracy, moral rectitude, legal legitimacy, and vindication. This root is the primary structural axis of the truth-as-correctness cluster in Georgian.

---

**Root 2**

**Form:** ჭეშმარ- / č̣ešmar-
**Transliteration:** č̣ešmar-
**P1 participation:** 2 items — č̣ešmariti (#1), č̣ešmariteba (#2)
**Core meaning contribution:** Truth as genuine quality or authentic correspondence to reality — the philosophically and theologically marked root for truth in its deepest or most absolute sense. Less productive morphologically than mart-, but semantically central to the domain.

---

**Root 3**

**Form:** ყალბ- / q̇alb-
**Transliteration:** q̇alb-
**P1 participation:** 2 items — q̇albi (#6), siq̇albe (#5)
**Core meaning contribution:** Falseness, counterfeit quality, and inauthenticity — the primary root for the negative pole of the truth domain, covering forgery, fraud, and spurious identity. Highly productive in legal and everyday registers.

**Transliteration:** martebulobā

**Natural English translation:** Orthodox (Christian); literally "right-glorifier"

**Natural English translation:** law, right, justice (as a system or body of norms)
**Context of use:** The standard Georgian term for law as a normative system, used in legal, academic, and institutional contexts. Distinct from kanoni (a specific law or rule) in referring to law as a whole domain or system.

## Step 3 — Peripheral Extensions

The following expressions involve the identified roots in contexts where the core truth-domain contribution appears to shift or extend into other semantic territory. These are flagged without interpretation or categorization.

---

**mart- root:**

- **მართლმადიდებელი** (martlmadidebeli): The mart- root here participates in the name of a religious confession (Eastern Orthodoxy), where the "right/true" component is fused with "glorifying" in a way that makes the truth-domain contribution inseparable from liturgical and doxological function.

- **მართლწერა** (martlwera): The root contributes to the domain of orthographic correctness — the "rightness" of written forms — which is a normative linguistic standard rather than a truth-evaluative judgment about states of affairs.

- **მართლზომიერება** (martlzomiereba): The root combines with a measure-concept to produce a proportionality principle in administrative and constitutional law, where "rightness" functions as a standard of degree rather than a binary truth value.

- **გამართლება** (gamartleba): In everyday usage, this form is frequently used to mean "making excuses" or "rationalizing," where the root's contribution shifts from genuine vindication toward motivated reasoning or self-justification.

- **მართება** (marteba) in the construction X-s marteba aqvs: The root here functions as a modal marker of obligation or fittingness rather than a descriptor of factual correctness.

- **სამართალი** (samart̕ali): The root generates the term for law as a normative system, where "rightness" becomes institutionalized as a body of rules rather than a property of individual statements or persons.

---

**č̣ešmar- root:**

- **ჭეშმარიტი ხელოვნება** (č̣ešmariti xelovneba): The root is applied to aesthetic evaluation of art, where "genuine" or "true" art is distinguished from imitation or commercial production — a domain of aesthetic judgment rather than propositional truth.

- **ჭეშმარიტი ბუნება** (č̣ešmariti buneba): The root is applied to the concept of essential nature, where "true" functions as a marker of essence or fundamental character rather than correspondence to fact.

- **ჭეშმარიტი მოწმე** (č̣ešmariti mowme): In theological usage, this phrase connects to the concept of martyrdom (Greek martys, "witness"), where the root's truth-domain contribution intersects with the domain of sacrificial testimony and religious identity.

---

**q̇alb- root:**

- **ყალბი ნოტა** (q̇albi not̕a): The root is applied to musical performance, where "false" describes a pitch error rather than a propositional falsehood — a domain of technical correctness in aesthetic execution.

- **ყალბი ნაბიჯი** (q̇albi nabiǰi): The root is applied metaphorically to conduct and decision-making, where "false step" describes an error in judgment or strategy rather than a false statement.

- **ყალბი სტარტი** (q̇albi st̕art̕i): The root is applied to procedural invalidity in competitive contexts (sports), where "false" marks a rule violation rather than a truth-evaluative judgment.

## Group 1: Terms used in legal proceedings to evaluate documents, signatures, seals, and physical evidence

**Label:** Expressions used to evaluate the integrity of physical and documentary evidence in legal and administrative contexts

**Definition:** These expressions appear consistently in legal, notarial, and administrative discourse when the question at issue is whether a document, signature, seal, currency, or other physical object is what it purports to be. They are used by courts, investigators, and administrative bodies to classify items as genuine or falsified. The contrast between the positive and negative poles of this group is highly institutionalized in Georgian criminal and administrative law.

**Representative expressions:**

- ყალბი დოკუმენტი / q̇albi dokumenti (forged document)

- სიყალბე / siq̇albe (falseness, inauthenticity — the abstract property)
- სიყალბის ნიშნები / siq̇albis nišnebi (signs of falseness)
- ნამდვილობა / namdviloba (authenticity — the property being verified)

- ნამდვილობის შემოწმება / namdvilobis šemowmeba (authenticity check)
- ავთენტური / avt̕ent̕uri (authentic — formal/archival register)
- ავთენტური ტექსტი / avt̕ent̕uri t̕eqst̕i (authentic text)
- ავთენტური ხელმოწერა / avt̕ent̕uri xelmowera (authentic signature)

Avt̕ent̕uri is restricted to formal and archival registers; namdvili covers the same ground in less formal usage. Kanonieri and ukanono appear in this group when the question is whether ownership or a claim is legally valid, rather than whether a physical object is genuine.

## Group 2: Terms used in legal proceedings to evaluate testimony and witnesses

**Label:** Expressions used to assess the truthfulness and reliability of witnesses and testimony

**Definition:** These expressions appear in legal proceedings — trials, investigations, depositions — when the question is whether a witness is telling the truth and whether their testimony can be relied upon. They are used by courts, lawyers, and investigators to classify witnesses and statements as credible or false. This group is distinct from Group 1 in that it concerns persons and verbal acts rather than physical objects.

## Group 3: Terms used in everyday speech to assert or deny that someone is lying

**Label:** Expressions used in everyday moral and interpersonal discourse to accuse, deny, or describe lying

**Definition:** These expressions appear in everyday spoken Georgian when speakers are making direct moral assessments of whether someone is lying or telling the truth. They are used in arguments, storytelling, and moral evaluation of persons. This group is characterized by high frequency in spoken registers and by participation in fixed verbal constructions with t̕q̇va (said) and amboba (to say/tell).

**Representative expressions:**

- ტყუილი / ẗq̇uili (lie — the most colloquial everyday term)

- მართლაც / martlac (indeed, truly — emphatic)

**Notes:** T̈q̇uili and sicrue overlap substantially in this group but ẗq̇uili is more colloquial and more frequent in direct accusation, while sicrue is slightly more abstract and appears more in moral reflection. The simartle constructions in this group (simartles vambob, simartle git̕xra, simartle rom vt̕q̇vat̕) function as performative or discourse-framing devices — they are not simply descriptions of truth-telling but acts of positioning oneself as honest in conversation. Martla and martlac are discourse particles that confirm or emphasize truth and are among the most frequent words in spoken Georgian.

**Label:** Expressions appearing in proverbial, literary, and moral discourse about truth and deception as forces or entities

**Definition:** These expressions appear in contexts where truth and lies are treated as agents or forces with characteristic behaviors — truth prevails, lies breed more lies, lies cannot stand. ## Group 7: Terms used to evaluate the correctness of statements, arguments, and reasoning

**Label:** Expressions used to evaluate whether statements, arguments, decisions, or conclusions are correct, well-founded, or accurate

**Definition:** These expressions appear when speakers or writers are assessing the epistemic quality of a claim, argument, or conclusion — whether it is accurate, well-founded, or free from error. They are used across formal and informal registers but are especially prominent in academic, journalistic, and legal argumentation. The contrast in this group is between correctness/accuracy and error/incorrectness, rather than between genuine and counterfeit (Group 5) or truthful and lying (Group 3).

**Representative expressions:**

- ზუსტი / zusti (exact, precise, accurate)
- სიზუსტე / sizuste (exactness, precision, accuracy)
- ზუსტად / zustad (exactly, precisely — also used as a confirmation particle)

**Notes:** Zusti and its derivatives are the primary terms for precision and accuracy in technical and scientific contexts. Martebuli is used specifically for well-foundedness of arguments and decisions — it implies that something has been correctly reasoned or appropriately applied, not merely that it is factually accurate. Mcdari is important within this group because it marks error without implying deliberate deception, distinguishing it from q̇albi (which implies intent to deceive). Šesabamisi overlaps with Group 6 but appears here when the question is whether a statement or conclusion is consistent with the evidence or with a prior claim. Martla and martlac function as confirmation particles in this group, asserting the accuracy of what has just been said.

- სარწმუნოების თავისუფლება / sarwmunoebis t̕avisup̕leba (freedom of religion)
- სარწმუნოების ნიშნით / sarwmunoebis nišnit̕ (on grounds of religion)
- მართლსაიდუმლო / martlsaidumlo (true sacrament — theological)
- ღმერთი მართალია / ɣmerti martalia (God is just/righteous)
- მართლი გზა / martli gza (the right path — in religious/moral usage)

**Notes:** The most significant observation here is the semantic bifurcation of sarwmunoeba: in secular contexts it means credibility/reliability, but in theological contexts it means faith/religion. These are not merely polysemous uses of the same word but distinct registers with distinct collocational patterns. Similarly, č̣ešmariteba in theological usage tends to refer to absolute or divine truth, while in everyday usage it refers to the truth of statements. Martlmadidebeli is the most institutionalized form in this group — it is the standard name for the dominant religious confession in Georgia and is not used outside religious and historical contexts.

## Group 9: Terms used to evaluate sincerity and authenticity of persons and their expressions

**Label:** Expressions used to evaluate whether a person's character, emotions, or expressions are genuine rather than performed or hypocritical

**Definition:** These expressions appear when speakers are assessing whether a person is genuinely what they appear to be — whether their emotions, friendship, or character are authentic rather than performed or deceptive. Unlike Group 1 (documents) or Group 3 (lying), this group concerns the authenticity of persons and their inner states as expressed outwardly. The contrast is between genuine character and performed or hypocritical presentation.

**Representative expressions:**

- გულწრფელი / gulwrp̕eli (sincere, genuine, frank — literally "straight-hearted")
- გულწრფელობა / gulwrp̕eloba (sincerity, genuineness, candor)
- გულწრფელად / gulwrp̕elad (sincerely, genuinely, frankly)
- თვალთმაქცობა / t̕valt̕maq̇c̕oba (deception through appearance, hypocrisy, charlatanism)
- თვალთმაქცი / t̕valt̕maq̇c̕i (deceiver, hypocrite, charlatan)
- ნამდვილი მეგობარი / namdvili megobari (a true friend)
- ჭეშმარიტი მეგობარი / č̣ešmariti megobari (a true friend — more literary)
- ჭეშმარიტი სიყვარული / č̣ešmariti siq̇varuli (true love)
- ყალბი ღიმილი / q̇albi ɣimili (a false smile)
- ყალბი პათოსი / q̇albi p̕at̕osi (false pathos, hollow rhetoric)
- მართალი ადამიანი / martali adamiani (a just, honest person)
- ნამდვილი ქართველი / namdvili q̇art̕veli (a real Georgian — authentic identity)
- გარეგნული / garegnuli (outward, superficial, apparent — implying contrast with inner reality)
- გარეგნობა / garegnoba (outward appearance, exterior)
- გარეგნულად / garegnulad (outwardly, superficially)

**Notes:** Gulwrp̕eli and t̕valt̕maq̇c̕oba are the clearest poles of this group: gulwrp̕eli marks genuine inner character expressed outwardly, while t̕valt̕maq̇c̕oba marks deliberate deception through outward performance. Garegnuli belongs here because it marks the outward/inner contrast that underlies the whole group — it is used precisely in contexts where the reliability of surface appearances is in question. The namdvili and č̣ešmariti collocations with megobari and siq̇varuli belong here rather than in Group 5 because the question is not material authenticity but the genuineness of a relationship or emotion.

## Group 10: Terms used in discourse about orthographic, linguistic, and procedural correctness

**Label:** Expressions used to evaluate correctness in linguistic, orthographic, and procedural domains

**Definition:** These expressions appear when the question is whether something conforms to a normative standard of correct form — correct spelling, correct speech, correct procedure. The "correctness" here is not factual accuracy (Group 7) or legal validity (Group 6) but conformity to a recognized norm of proper form. This group is smaller and more specialized than the others.

**Representative expressions:**

- მართლწერა / martlwera (orthography, correct spelling)
- მართლწერის წესები / martlweris wesesbi (rules of orthography)
- მართლმეტყველება / martlmet̕q̇veleba (correct speech, orthoepy)
- ზუსტი / zusti (exact, precise — also used for accurate translations and measurements)
- სიზუსტე / sizuste (exactness, precision)
- შესაბამისი / šesabamisi (conforming, consistent with — when applied to procedural compliance)
- მართებული / martebuli (appropriate, correct — when applied to usage or procedure)
- არსებითი სახელი / arsebiti saxeli (noun — grammatical term; literally "essential name")

**Notes:** This group is identified because the mart- root generates a distinct cluster of terms specifically for linguistic and orthographic correctness (martlwera, martlmet̕q̇veleba) that do not appear in the other groups. Zusti appears here when applied to translations and measurements, overlapping with Group 7. Arsebiti saxeli is included as a fixed grammatical term that uses arsebiti in a specialized technical sense distinct from its philosophical usage.

## Ambiguous and overlapping items

The following items appear in multiple groups and cannot be assigned to a single group without distorting the observed usage patterns:

**სიმართლე / simartle** — Appears in Group 3 (everyday assertions of truth-telling), Group 4 (proverbial discourse), and Group 7 (evaluating correctness of statements). The term is the most versatile in the domain and resists single-group assignment. Its discourse-framing constructions (simartle git̕xra, simartle rom vt̕q̇vat̕) are specific to Group 3; its proverbial constructions (simartles ver gaekceviˈ) belong to Group 4; its factual assertion constructions (simartle isaa, rom...) belong to Group 7.

**ჭეშმარიტება / č̣ešmariteba** — Appears in Group 4 (proverbial/moral discourse), Group 8 (theological discourse), and Group 7 (philosophical discourse about truth). The term is the most philosophically and theologically marked word for truth in Georgian and participates in all three of these registers.

**მართალი / martali** — Appears in Group 3 (everyday assertions: martali xar, martalia magram), Group 6 (legal/moral: martali adamiani), and Group 8 (theological: ɣmerti martalia). The adverbial derivatives martla and martlac belong most clearly to Group 3.

**სარწმუნო / sarwmuno** — Appears in Group 2 (legal evaluation of witnesses and sources) and Group 8 (through its derivative sarwmunoeba in the theological sense of faith/religion). The two registers are clearly distinct in usage.

**შესაბამისი / šesabamisi** — Appears in Group 6 (institutional/legal conformity), Group 7 (consistency of statements with evidence), and Group 10 (procedural correctness). The term is highly productive across formal registers.

**კანონიერი / kanonieri** — Appears in Group 1 (legal validity of documents and claims) and Group 6 (lawfulness of authority and actions). The distinction is between evaluating a specific item (Group 1) and evaluating a system or course of conduct (Group 6).

**ნამდვილი / namdvili** — Appears in Group 5 (commercial/material authenticity), Group 9 (authenticity of persons and relationships), and overlaps with Group 1 through namdviloba (formal authentication). The term is the most productive adjective for genuineness across all registers.

**ყალბი / q̇albi** — Appears in Group 1 (forged documents), Group 2 (false testimony), Group 3 (lying), Group 5 (fake objects), and Group 9 (false emotional expression). The term is the most productive adjective for falseness/fakeness across all registers.

**გამართლება / gamartleba** — Appears in Group 2 (legal acquittal/vindication) and Group 6 (justification of authority or action), and also in everyday usage meaning "making excuses" which does not fit cleanly into any group. The documentation notes this semantic range explicitly.

**მიმსგავსება / mimsgavseba** — The documentation marks this as [MARGINAL] and notes it appears in aesthetic and theological contexts (resemblance to a divine model). It does not participate in any of the observed usage clusters with sufficient frequency to warrant group membership.

**უმსგავსო / umsgavso** — The documentation notes that in older literary Georgian this term carries the sense of "unseemly" or "not fitting," which is a normative use of the similarity concept. This is not sufficiently attested in current usage to warrant group placement.

**არსებითი / arsebiti** — In its philosophical sense (essential, fundamental), this term does not fit clearly into any group. Its legal use (arsebiti gansxvaveba, "material difference") overlaps with Group 6, and its grammatical use (arsebiti saxeli, "noun") belongs to Group 10, but the philosophical core meaning is not strongly represented in any group's usage patterns.

**მართება / marteba** (in the modal construction X-s marteba aqvs) — The documentation notes that this construction functions as a modal marker of obligation or fittingness. This is a peripheral use of the mart- root that does not fit the truth/falseness domain of the other groups.

**ტყუილუბრალოდ / ẗq̇uilubralod and ტყუილად / ẗq̇uilad** — These adverbial forms carry the "in vain, for nothing" sense of ẗq̇uili rather than the "lie/falsehood" sense. They do not fit into any of the groups above, which are organized around truth and falseness rather than futility or purposelessness.
